opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think "foundational" has become one of the most overloaded words in the field. Everyone wants their model to be the foundation model for biology, and the term gets used more as a marketing claim than a technical one. So I try to strip the label away and ask a few practical questions.

First: does the model let you do something you couldn't do before? Not "it beats the previous benchmark by two points," but does it unlock a genuinely new capability? Can it generate a functional protein or a working genetic element that a scientist would have struggled to design by hand? Can it make a prediction that changes what experiment you run next?

Second, and this is the big one for me: does it hold up in the wet lab? Biology is unforgiving. You can get beautiful in-silico metrics, perplexity curves going down, nice benchmark tables, and then you synthesize the designs and very few of them work. The real test is a closed loop, where you design something, build it, measure it, and the model's hit rate is meaningfully better than the alternatives. Experimental validation has to be the currency.

Third: how well does it generalize? A lot of models do well on in-distribution held-out data that's basically a close cousin of the training set. That's not very interesting. I want to see what happens when you push it into new regions of sequence space, new organisms, new functions. That's where you learn whether it has captured something real about biology or just memorized the evolutionary record.

And finally, is it actually being used? The best signal of value is whether other labs, people with no stake in your success, pick it up and build on it. If a model becomes infrastructure that people reach for in their own work, that's foundational in the meaningful sense. If it's mostly cited in competing press releases, it isn't.

The hard part is that the field doesn't yet have the equivalent of ImageNet or the language benchmarks that let everyone compare apples to apples. Biological benchmarks are fragmented, often leaky, and frequently disconnected from what matters experimentally. So I think one of the most valuable things the community can do right now is build shared, rigorous evaluations tied to real experimental outcomes. Then a lot of the arguments about whose model is more foundational would settle themselves, because the data would answer the question.

r001.rationale: The response says valuable models may become infrastructure that other labs build on, but it does not describe an ecosystem of applications or compare one to an app store.

r002.rationale: It recommends stripping away the “foundational” label and judging models by practical value, including whether they unlock useful capabilities and improve experiments.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "foundational" has become a bit of a marketing word, and I try not to get too caught up in it. The question I actually care about is: what can you do with the model that you couldn't do before? That's the only test that matters.

Biology is different from language in an important way. With text, there's a reasonably tight loop between the model and the thing it's modeling. In biology, the model is a hypothesis generator, and the ground truth lives in a wet lab. So when someone tells me their model is more foundational, my first question is, what did you measure? Did you design a protein and express it? Did you edit a genome and sequence the result? Did the prediction hold up at the bench? A benchmark score on a held-out set is a starting point, but it's not the finish line.

The second thing I look at is whether the model generalizes to things that are genuinely new. A lot of models look great when you evaluate them on sequences that resemble their training data, and then fall apart on an organism or a protein family that's underrepresented. The truly interesting models are the ones that have learned something about the underlying rules, so they can make useful predictions in regions of sequence space nobody has looked at carefully.

And then there's the practical question of whether anyone else actually uses it. Foundational models, in the sense that term originally meant, are the ones other people build on. If a model gets released and a year later there are hundreds of labs fine-tuning it, wrapping it, using it as a starting point for their own problems, that tells you something real. That adoption is hard to fake.

So I'd say: care less about the claims, care more about the experiments, the generalization, and whether the community votes with its feet. The field moves fast enough that the leaderboard arguments will sort themselves out. What won't sort itself out is whether we're actually curing diseases or engineering biology better than we were before. That's the scoreboard I keep looking at.

r001.rationale: The response says other labs build on, fine-tune, and wrap released models, but it does not describe an ecosystem of applications analogous to an app store.

r002.rationale: It says the key question is what the model enables that could not be done before and urges judging useful capabilities over claims of being foundational.

astra-6.text:
I think the question is: what does the model let you do that you couldn’t do before? Calling something a foundation model isn’t, by itself, evidence that it’s useful. Can it predict the outcome of an experiment? Can it help you design a molecule or a biological system with a property you actually care about? And when you take that prediction into the lab, does it work?

Benchmarks are useful, but in biology you have to be very careful about what they’re measuring. A model can look great on held-out data that’s still very similar to its training data. The harder test is whether it generalizes to a new biological context, or helps you choose an experiment whose outcome you don’t already know.

So I’d focus less on whose model is more foundational and more on prospective experimental validation. Does it make discovery faster, cheaper, or possible at all? That’s where the value becomes concrete.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe an ecosystem of applications built on foundational models or compare it to an app store.

r002.rationale: It says to focus on what the model lets researchers do and that calling it foundational is not evidence of usefulness.

sol-6.1.text:
I think “foundational” is something you earn through usefulness, rather than something you declare about your model. Does it help you predict biology you haven’t seen before? Can it guide an experiment that actually works? Can somebody who didn’t build the model use it to make a discovery?

The important distinction is between doing well on a benchmark and changing what you can do in the lab. Biology gives you this wonderful reality check: you can make a prediction, run the experiment, and see whether you were right. So I care less about who has the most foundational model and more about whether these models let us ask—and answer—questions that we couldn’t before.

r001.rationale: The response does not describe an ecosystem of applications built on foundational models or compare one to an app store.

r002.rationale: It says foundational status is earned through usefulness and emphasizes whether models enable useful predictions, experiments, and discoveries over benchmark performance or claims of being foundational.
